# Ocular motility disorders and strabismus

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Ophthalmic surgery > Ocular motility disorders and strabismus*

[Original Article Link](/library/uO0p8T)

---

## Summary

<u>Strabismus</u> is a condition characterized by misalignment of the eyes when looking at an object. One <u>eye</u> deviates (either constantly or intermittently) from the normal visual axis, which results in the inability of the <u>brain</u> to fuse together the images from the right and left <u>eye</u>. <u>Strabismus</u> is classified as either concomitant (nonparalytic) or paralytic. <u>Concomitant strabismus</u> primarily occurs in early childhood and manifests with a constant angle of deviation, in which the misaligned <u>eye</u> follows the unaffected <u>eye</u>. <u>Paralytic strabismus</u> is frequently acquired and is due to the <u>functional weakness</u> of individual <u>extraocular muscles</u>, which alter the angle of deviation depending on the direction of view. Further typical features include double as well as decreased <u>vision</u>. Treatment at an early stage (e.g., via <u>occlusion treatment</u> or <u>surgery</u>) is essential to prevent complications such as <u>amblyopia</u> (decreased <u>vision</u> in an <u>eye</u> with no apparent structural abnormality) and loss of binocular <u>vision</u>. Further complex ocular motility disorders can result from central nervous pathologies. <u>Internuclear ophthalmoplegia</u>, for example, is caused by a lesion of the <u>medial longitudinal fasciculus</u> and causes disturbances in horizontal <u>eye movements</u>.

---

## Basic terms

* Strabismus: abnormal alignment of the eyes; the visual axes of the eyes are not parallel (crossed-eyes)

* Heterotropia: manifest <u>strabismus</u> 

* Esotropia: inward misalignment (most common type in children)

* Exotropia: outward misalignment

* Hypertropia: upward deviation of one <u>eye</u>

* Hypotropia: downward deviation of one <u>eye</u>

* Cyclotropia: rotation of one <u>eye</u> around an <u>anterior-posterior axis</u>

* Heterophoria: latent <u>strabismus</u>  ; presents with the same (latent) misalignments seen in <u>heterotropia</u>.

* Esophoria: a type of <u>heterophoria</u> in which one <u>eye</u> has a tendency to converge towards the nose when the other <u>eye</u> is shut; the opposite of <u>exophoria</u>

* Exophoria: a type of <u>heterophoria</u> in which one <u>eye</u> has a tendency to deviate away from the nose when the other <u>eye</u> is shut; the opposite of <u>esophoria</u>

* Brown syndrome: a rare form of <u>strabismus</u> that presents with limited elevation of the affected <u>eye</u>

## Concomitant strabismus

### Definition



* <u>Strabismus</u> in which the degree of deviation (angle between the visual axes of both the eyes) remains constant in all directions of gaze




### Etiology




* Genetic

* Uncorrected <u>refractive error</u> (particularly <u>hyperopia</u> and <u>anisometropia</u>)

* Unilateral visual impairment/<u>amblyopia</u> (e.g., organic causes, retinal disease, <u>retinoblastoma</u>)

* Other: <u>perinatal</u> lesions (e.g., <u>preterm birth</u>, <u>asphyxia</u>), cerebral damage (e.g., trauma, <u>encephalitis</u>)





### Types




* Congenital or infantile <u>concomitant strabismus</u>

* Evident at <u>birth</u> or onset within 6 months of age ; does not resolve spontaneously

* May manifest as <u>esotropia</u> or <u>exotropia</u>

* Microstrabismus: angle of deviation < 5°; therefore frequently a late diagnosis with high risk of <u>amblyopia</u>

* Latent <u>strabismus</u>: usually no clinical significance; the deviation is compensated by fixation (fusion); decompensation and manifestation occur in situations of physical <u>stress</u>.





### Diagnostics




* Hirschberg test; : a test for determining if the eyes are in alignment. A light is shone at the eyes and the location of the light reflex on the <u>cornea</u> is observed in reference to the <u>pupil</u>. Asymmetrical corneal reflections on <u>examination of the eyes</u> indicate that the visual axes are not aligned (<u>strabismus</u>).

* <u>Cover tests</u> (see “<u>Cover test</u>s” in “<u>Examination of the eyes</u>”)

* Measurement of the angle of deviation: if necessary with the help of a tangent screen





### Therapeutic options




The main goals in <u>strabismus</u> management are to optimize <u>visual acuity</u> and achieve binocularity.




* Correction of <u>refractive errors</u>

* Visual training therapy

* Training to correct <u>eye movements</u> (e.g., in <u>strabismus</u>) and visual-motor deficiencies

* Uses specialized computer and <u>optical devices</u> (e.g., lenses and prisms)

* Occlusion treatment 

* Initiate as early as possible!

* Cover the unaffected <u>eye</u> using a patch (occlusion) → training of the weaker <u>eye</u>

* Duration of coverage depends on the child's age

* Penalization therapy (<u>cyclopentolate</u> drop therapy): : apply <u>cyclopentolate</u> drops ;   to the unaffected <u>eye</u> → blurs <u>vision</u> → encourages monocular use of the affected <u>eye</u>

* <u>Botulinum toxin</u> therapy : toxin injection into the stronger muscle → temporary and partial <u>paralysis</u> → weaker muscle forced to contract → long-lasting alteration in ocular alignment

* Strabismus surgery 

* Transposition or repositioning of muscles

* Tucking or advancement  to tighten muscles

* Myectomy or tenectomy to loosen <u>extraocular muscles</u>





### Complications




* Disturbances of binocular <u>vision</u>

* Amblyopia

* Definition: visual decrease in one or both eyes (functional visual impairment) due to a developmental <u>vision</u> disorder during early childhood

* Pathophysiology: one or both eyes convey poor or mismatched visual information to the <u>brain</u> → <u>brain</u> suppresses information from one or both eyes → disuse of the <u>eye</u> → lacking visual stimuli with partial underdevelopment of the <u>visual cortex</u>

* Forms

* Deprivation amblyopia (e.g., via <u>ptosis</u>, <u>cataract</u>, occlusion)

* Refractive amblyopia

* Strabismus amblyopia





> [!WARNING]
> Failure to detect or adequately treat <u>strabismus</u> may result in irreversible <u>amblyopia</u>!




> [!NOTE]
> A serious underlying condition (e.g., <u>brain tumor</u>) should be suspected in <u>infants</u> with <u>strabismus</u>, especially in the presence of additional ocular findings like <u>leukocoria</u>!

## Paralytic strabismus

### Definition




* <u>Strabismus</u> caused by <u>paresis</u> (partial failure of action) or <u>paralysis</u> (total failure of action) of one or more <u>extraocular muscles</u> (ophthalmoplegia)

* The angle of deviation alters depending on the direction of gaze (incomitant <u>strabismus</u>)





### Etiology




* Neuropathies: 3<sup>rd</sup>, 4<sup>th</sup>, and 6<sup>th</sup><u>cranial</u> nerve palsies (see <u>cranial nerve disorders</u>)

* <u>Demyelinating</u> disease (e.g., <u>multiple sclerosis</u>)

* <u>Myopathies</u> (e.g., <u>myasthenia gravis</u>, ocular <u>myopathies</u>, restrictive <u>thyroid</u> <u>myopathy</u>)

* Microangiopathic vasculopathy (often related to <u>diabetes</u> and <u>hypertension</u>)

* Trauma

* Intracranial or intraorbital masses

* Congenital in rare cases (e.g., overaction of the <u>inferior oblique muscles</u>)





### Clinical features




* Diplopia (<u>double vision</u>): most pronounced when looking in the direction usually enabled by the paralyzed muscle

* Often compensatory head posture

* Impaired <u>extraocular muscle</u> function





> [!NOTE]
> Patients with poor <u>visual acuity</u> may not notice <u>diplopia</u>. Therefore, complete optical (refractory) correction must be achieved before testing for <u>strabismus</u>!




### Diagnosis




* Horizontal <u>paralytic strabismus</u>

* <u>Exotropia</u> → <u>medial rectus</u> <u>weakness</u> → <u>oculomotor nerve palsy</u>

* <u>Esotropia</u> → <u>lateral rectus</u> <u>weakness</u> → <u>abducens nerve palsy</u>

* Vertical <u>paralytic strabismus</u>: perform a 3-step Park-Bielchowsky test





| Steps | Inference | Underlying principle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <br><u>Step 1</u>: Determine which <u>eye</u> is <u>hypertropic</u> in <u>primary gaze</u>. | <br><br>* <u>Hypertropic</u> right <u>eye</u> → <u>weakness</u> of right <u>eye</u> depressors or left <u>eye</u> elevators<br><br>* <u>Hypertropic</u> left <u>eye</u> → <u>weakness</u> of right <u>eye</u> elevators or left <u>eye</u> depressors<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Elevators: <u>inferior oblique</u>, <u>superior rectus</u><br><br>* Depressors: <u>inferior rectus</u>, <u>superior oblique</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Step 2</u>: Determine whether <u>hypertropia</u> increases on the right or left gaze. | <br><br>* Vertical <u>strabismus</u> increases on looking right  → <u>weakness</u> of right <u>superior rectus</u>, right <u>inferior rectus</u>, left superior obliquus, or left inferior obliquus<br><br>* Vertical <u>strabismus</u> increases on looking left  → <u>weakness</u> of right superior obliquus, right inferior obliquus, left <u>superior rectus</u>, or left <u>inferior rectus</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Superior and <u>inferior rectus muscles</u> have their greatest vertical action when the <u>eye</u> is <u>abducted</u>.<br><br>* Superior and <u>inferior oblique muscles</u> have their greatest vertical action when the <u>eye</u> is <u>adducted</u>.<br><br><br> |
| <br>Step 3: Determine whether <u>hypertropia</u> increases on right or left head tilt. | <br><br>* Vertical <u>strabismus</u> increases on tilting the head towards the right shoulder  → <u>weakness</u> of a right <u>eye</u> intorter or a left <u>eye</u> extorter<br><br>* Vertical <u>strabismus</u> increases on lilting the head towards the left shoulder  → <u>weakness</u> of a left <u>eye</u> intorter or right <u>eye</u> extorter<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Intorters: <u>superior oblique</u>, <u>superior rectus</u><br><br>* Extorters: <u>inferior rectus</u>, <u>inferior oblique</u><br><br><br> |





| Weak <u>extraocular muscle</u> | <br><u>Step 1</u>: Which <u>eye</u> is <u>hypertropic</u>?<br> | <br><u>Step 2</u>: Vertical <u>strabismus</u> increases with <u>lateral</u> gaze in this directon<br> | <br>Step 3: Vertical <u>strabismus</u> increases with head-tilt towards this shoulder |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Right <u>superior oblique</u> | Right <u>eye</u><br> | Left <u>lateral</u> gaze | Right shoulder |
| Left <u>superior oblique</u> | Left <u>eye</u><br> | Right <u>lateral</u> gaze | Left shoulder |





### Treatment




* Correction of <u>refractive errors</u>

* Prismatic glasses

* Treatment of underlying cause

* <u>Strabismus surgery</u>

## Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)

### Definition




* Damage to the <u>medial longitudinal fasciculus</u> (the connection between the abducens <u>nucleus</u>, <u>CN VI</u>, on one side and the oculomotor <u>nucleus</u>, <u>CN III</u>, on the other), which leads to impaired <u>lateral</u> gaze.

* Manifests primarily with impaired <u>adduction</u> of the <u>eye</u> <u>ipsilateral</u> to the lesion (<u>ipsilateral</u> to the <u>medial longitudinal fasciculus</u> lesion)

* Depending on which <u>eye</u> is affected, <u>INO</u> is classified as left, right, or bilateral





### Etiology




* <u>Multiple sclerosis</u> (MS)

* Common cause in individuals with <u>INO</u> between 20–50 years of age [[11]](/library/G-YBA7)

* Typically bilateral

* <u>Infarction</u> (common cause in older patients)

* Rare causes: <u>brain tumors</u>, chronic <u>alcohol</u> and <u>recreational drug</u> use, <u>encephalitis</u>, metabolic disorders





### Pathophysiology




* Physiologically, <u>CN VI</u> receives a signal from the <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>paramedian pontine reticular formation</u> and sends a signal to the <u>contralateral</u> <u>CN III</u> via the <u>medial longitudinal fasciculus</u>.

* Activation of the <u>CN VI</u> → activation of the <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>lateral rectus</u> → <u>abduction</u> of the <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>eye</u>

* Activation of the <u>CN III</u> → activation of the <u>contralateral</u> <u>medial</u> rectus → <u>adduction</u> of the <u>contralateral</u> <u>eye</u>

* Disruption of the <u>medial longitudinal fasciculus</u> fibers linking the <u>CN VI</u> <u>contralateral</u> and the <u>CN III</u> <u>ipsilateral</u> to the lesion → failure of signal transmission from <u>CN VI</u> to <u>CN III</u> → the <u>contralateral</u> <u>lateral rectus</u> is activated while the <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>medial rectus</u> is not → <u>abduction</u> of the <u>contralateral</u> <u>eye</u>, no <u>adduction</u> of <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>eye</u>

* Firing from <u>CN VI</u> which fails to be transmitted to <u>CN III</u> is instead partially transmitted to the <u>lateral rectus</u> <u>contralateral</u> to the lesion → <u>nystagmus</u> of the <u>contralateral</u> <u>abducting</u> <u>eye</u>





![Internuclear ophthalmoplegia](media/nbxag296wcj2x85kbyyy6iwa.jpg)

Internuclear ophthalmoplegia

![Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia](media/small_6001a880204af.jpg)

Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia




### Clinical findings




* <u>Adduction</u> limited in horizontal <u>eye movements</u>

* <u>Adduction</u> is retained in <u>convergence</u> reaction

* <u>Dissociated nystagmus</u>: gaze to the opposite side → <u>nystagmus</u> of the <u>abducted</u> <u>contralateral</u> <u>eye</u>

* In bilateral <u>INO</u>: possible <u>vertical nystagmus</u>





> [!NOTE]
> Remember that <u>internuclear ophthalmoplegia</u> (<u>INO</u>) is characterized by Impaired <u>adduction</u> of the <u>eye</u> <u>ipsilateral</u> to the lesion and Nystagmus on the Opposite side!




![Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)](media/y6ay2t8rc2jm07lor60k88pw.jpg)
